blocks.heading: The week of yiras Hashem and the start of teshuvah

paragraphs.text: The Mashgiach opens with parshas Eikev and its call 'What does Hashem ask of you, but to fear Hashem'. Of the seven weeks of comfort before Rosh Hashanah, the first is the week of love of Hashem and this week is the week of fear, as the haftarah's 'Who among you fears Hashem' shows. Rebbe Reb Bunim, he relates, learned Sefer Devarim as his mussar, above all parshas Eikev.

The talmidim of the Ba'al Shem Tov said that the days of teshuvah begin on the fifteenth of Av, and the Mishnah counts that day among Klal Yisrael's greatest yamim tovim. A person who feels he lacks yiras shamayim, the Mashgiach says, has here a time to draw it.

blocks.heading: A shidduch between Hashem and Klal Yisrael

paragraphs.text: The day of shidduchim, the Mashgiach explains, is also a shidduch between Hashem and Klal Yisrael, who in galus say 'Do not look at me for I am dark'. As before any shidduch, one must look over the tenaim, and these tenaim are the passuk: to fear Hashem, walk in His ways, love Him and serve Him with all one's heart and soul.
He urges reflecting on the whole parshah and its words that Hashem desired the Avos and chose their children after them. He then tells a story of a Chernobyler tzaddik.

Every match is announced from heaven, the Mashgiach says, yet one must merit to receive it. He brings a story told about a man in Biala who, on his way home on motza'ei Yom Kippur, would pick out a sealed box in the shop, open it only in the morning, and always have the finest in town. Asked about it, he said it was no wonder: what a Jew needs is set aside for him in heaven, and right after Yom Kippur, free of sin, his choice is good.

blocks.heading: Yom Kippur begins on Chamishah Asar b'Av

paragraphs.text: Choosing is hard, the Mashgiach notes, since a person's ruchniyus and even his gashmiyus are for the sake of Torah and avodas Hashem. Yom Kippur atones from beginning to end, so on that day a Jew's nature and choice incline to good. The avodah of teshuvah that ends on Yom Kippur begins on Chamishah Asar b'Av, and since the end lies in the beginning, Yom Kippur is already present then.

On this day, then, a Jew has a pull toward good and a desire for Hashem, as the Avos did, and his choice is at its best. The Mashgiach ties this to 'u'vacharta ba'chaim', choose life, and to the call to the young man to lift his eyes: to choose a path of life, a Torah of life.

blocks.heading: Av, Yerushalayim and a fear born of wholeness

paragraphs.text: The Beis Hamikdash in Yerushalayim, 'the joy of all the earth', was a place of simcha for the whole world, and the month of Av was its time of simcha. When Yerushalayim was destroyed, place and time turned to mourning: 'When Av enters, joy is lessened'. On Chamishah Asar b'Av the rebuilding of Yerushalayim begins.

Chazal call Yerushalayim 'yirah shleimah', a complete fear, and Avraham called it a place of fear. Ordinary fear comes from lack, as one fears a lion whose strength he lacks. Holy fear of Hashem comes from wholeness, not from lack.

blocks.heading: Why avodah in galus is so precious

paragraphs.text: The Gemara gives several reasons for Chamishah Asar b'Av and says to add in learning from then, but the Mashgiach sees a deep inner meaning not yet fully grasped. Some matters, as the Arizal said, may be revealed only as Moshiach draws near. Relying on the Chiddushei HaRim, he says the redemption could have come long ago, but Hashem cherishes the avodah of Jews in galus.

The Pesikta on 'Sing, O barren one' says the churban brought forth more tzaddikim than the Beis Hamikdash. Plainly the prophets were greater; yet the Arizal told R' Chaim Vital he surpassed earlier giants, because in so lowly a time his Torah was more precious. So the Pesikta means: those who cling to Yiddishkeit through hester panim are greater in Hashem's eyes than the tzaddikim of the Bayis era.

blocks.heading: The two sides of Tisha b'Av

paragraphs.text: The Chiddushei HaRim, rising from shivah on Chamishah Asar b'Av, linked the day to the Gemara that the dying of the generation of the desert then ended. The Mashgiach asks why the end of mourning would be a yom tov, which is done nowhere else.

Tisha b'Av, he answers, holds two opposites. It mourns the churban and hester panim, which grow each year, as the Chasam Sofer says, since 'every generation in whose days it is not rebuilt' suffers anew. Yet our avodah became more precious. On Tisha b'Av one cannot rejoice in that, for Hashem's honor requires the Beis Hamikdash.

The Chasam Sofer writes that for us galus is better, since in the 'days with no desire' there is no difficulty in serving Hashem; we pray for Moshiach only for the honor of Heaven. Hence, once the mourning ends, Chamishah Asar b'Av was set as a day to rejoice that, small as we are, we are precious to Hashem, and to make a reckoning: Moshiach may come tomorrow, so one must grab more Torah and mitzvos now.

blocks.heading: Adding in Torah from Chamishah Asar b'Av

paragraphs.text: The Navi cries 'Nachamu, nachamu ami', and Moshiach may come any moment. The Gemara's call to add in learning, the Mashgiach says, is not because nights grow longer; rather, with each year's new hester panim our avodah is more precious than before. Chamishah Asar b'Av is rising from the mourning to see the good the churban brought.

One must always pray for the Beis Hamikdash and await it daily; yet one may reckon that while it is not rebuilt, one should add in Torah, hard as learning is today, in tefillah and in every carefulness.
